variants.title: Trace an indexing request
variants.context: Elasticsearch routes each document to one primary shard, applies it there, forwards it to replicas, acknowledges per the active-copy contract, and makes it searchable only after a refresh publishes a segment.
variants.prompt: A product document is indexed. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Resolve the write alias and hash the routing value to one primary shard.
Apply the change on the primary and forward it to assigned replicas.
Acknowledge according to the active-copy and timeout contract.
Refresh so a searchable segment exposes the new version.

variants.hint: Search visibility is the last step, not the acknowledgement.
variants.explanation: Route → primary → acknowledge → refresh. A document can be acknowledged and durable before any search can see it.

variants.title: Trace an indexing request
variants.context: Elasticsearch routes each document to one primary shard, applies it there, forwards it to replicas, acknowledges per the active-copy contract, and makes it searchable only after a refresh publishes a segment.
variants.prompt: A write returns a timeout. Reconstruct the path in order.

items.text: The coordinator routed the document to its primary shard.
The primary applied it and forwarded to replicas.
The acknowledgement contract could not be satisfied within the deadline.
A later refresh may still expose the version if the write committed.

variants.hint: A timeout does not by itself prove whether the write committed.
variants.explanation: The write may have been applied. Treat the timeout as ambiguous and use stable IDs and versions so a retry replaces the same logical document.

variants.title: Trace an indexing request
variants.context: Elasticsearch routes each document to one primary shard, applies it there, forwards it to replicas, acknowledges per the active-copy contract, and makes it searchable only after a refresh publishes a segment.
variants.prompt: A client indexes a document and immediately searches for it but gets no hit. Put the steps in order, including why.

items.text: The document was routed and applied on its primary.
Replicas received the operation.
The write was acknowledged as durable per the contract.
No refresh has run yet, so no segment exposes it to search.

variants.hint: Near real time means visibility waits for a refresh.
variants.explanation: Refresh is not the same as a durable flush or snapshot; it is what makes indexed changes searchable.

variants.title: Map the field
variants.context: A mapping is a query contract. text is analyzed for relevance; keyword keeps one exact term for filters, grouping, and sorting; a multi-field indexes both; numeric and date types enable ranges and date math.
variants.prompt: Product category values must drive exact filters, facets, and sorting. Which field type?
optionFeedback: keyword keeps the whole value as one term for filters, grouping, and ordering.
text is analyzed into words, which breaks exact facets and ordinary terms aggregations.
Dynamic mapping can guess text plus keyword, but production mappings should be explicit.
variants.hint: Do you need words, or the whole value?
variants.explanation: Exact values belong in keyword fields. A normalizer can standardize case without tokenizing.

variants.title: Map the field
variants.context: A mapping is a query contract. text is analyzed for relevance; keyword keeps one exact term for filters, grouping, and sorting; a multi-field indexes both; numeric and date types enable ranges and date math.
variants.prompt: A product title must support relevance search and also exact facets on the full title. Which mapping?
options: A multi-field: text for relevance plus a keyword subfield.
optionFeedback: One source string indexed twice serves both questions.
text alone cannot facet or sort on the exact title.
keyword alone cannot rank on words inside the title.
variants.hint: Two different questions need two access paths.
variants.explanation: Index the string as text and as a keyword subfield. Each structure answers the question it was built for.

variants.title: Map the field
variants.context: A mapping is a query contract. text is analyzed for relevance; keyword keeps one exact term for filters, grouping, and sorting; a multi-field indexes both; numeric and date types enable ranges and date math.
variants.prompt: Prices were mapped as strings and range queries are wrong. What is the fix?
options: Create a new index generation with a numeric type and reindex.
Update the existing field type in place.
Add a range filter on the string field.
optionFeedback: A field type is hard to reverse; plan a new generation and reindex through the same transformer.
Existing segments keep the structures written under the old mapping.
String ranges compare lexically; “9” sorts after “10”.
variants.hint: Which mapping changes can be made without a new index?
variants.explanation: Treat mapping and analyzer changes as a new index generation. Typed values enable correct ranges, date math, and numeric aggregations.

variants.title: Size the shards
variants.context: Capacity arithmetic: future primary bytes = current + daily growth × days; average shard bytes = future primary bytes ÷ primary shards; stored bytes = primary bytes × (1 + replicas) × overhead; bytes per node = stored ÷ data nodes.
variants.prompt: Primary data is 400 GB and grows 5 GB per day. You plan for 60 days across 20 primary shards. What is the average primary shard size?
variants.hint: Future primary bytes first, then divide by shard count.
variants.explanation: 400 + 5 × 60 = 700 GB. 700 ÷ 20 = 35 GB per primary shard, inside Elastic’s rough 10–50 GB starting range.

mistakes.feedback: That divides today’s 400 GB; the plan must include 60 days of growth.
That is the total future primary size, not the per-shard average.

variants.title: Size the shards
variants.context: Capacity arithmetic: future primary bytes = current + daily growth × days; average shard bytes = future primary bytes ÷ primary shards; stored bytes = primary bytes × (1 + replicas) × overhead; bytes per node = stored ÷ data nodes.
variants.prompt: Future primary data is 700 GB with one replica and a measured index overhead factor of 1.2. How many GB will be stored?
variants.hint: Multiply primary bytes by copies, then by overhead.

mistakes.feedback: That forgets the measured 1.2 overhead factor.

variants.title: Size the shards
variants.context: Capacity arithmetic: future primary bytes = current + daily growth × days; average shard bytes = future primary bytes ÷ primary shards; stored bytes = primary bytes × (1 + replicas) × overhead; bytes per node = stored ÷ data nodes.
variants.prompt: Stored bytes total 1,680 GB across 6 data nodes. What is the average per data node?
variants.hint: Divide stored bytes by the number of data nodes.
variants.explanation: 1,680 ÷ 6 = 280 GB per node before disk watermarks and recovery headroom.

mistakes.feedback: Divide by the six data nodes.
That divides by eight nodes; the cluster has six.

variants.title: Read the cluster
variants.context: Green means every shard copy is assigned. Yellow means all primaries are assigned but a replica is not; data is searchable with reduced redundancy. A primary and its replica cannot occupy the same node.
variants.prompt: A single-node cluster reports yellow for an index with one replica. What does that mean?
options: Primaries are assigned but the replica cannot be placed on the same node as its primary.
optionFeedback: A replica needs a second node; until then redundancy is reduced but data is searchable.
Yellow means all primaries are assigned; nothing is missing.
Yellow does not block reads or writes.
variants.hint: Where can a replica copy live?
variants.explanation: Yellow is reduced redundancy. Add a data node or set replicas to zero for a single-node cluster.

variants.title: Read the cluster
variants.context: Green means every shard copy is assigned. Yellow means all primaries are assigned but a replica is not; data is searchable with reduced redundancy. A primary and its replica cannot occupy the same node.
variants.prompt: A node holding a primary shard fails. What happens next?
options: An in-sync replica is promoted to primary; the cluster is yellow until a new replica is assigned.
Searches fail until the node returns.
optionFeedback: Promotion keeps the shard writable; recovery restores redundancy afterwards.
Data survives on the replica copy.
The promoted replica keeps serving searches.
variants.hint: What is a replica for, besides read capacity?
variants.explanation: Replicas improve availability: one is promoted after a primary failure. They still do not replace an independent backup.

variants.title: Read the cluster
variants.context: Green means every shard copy is assigned. Yellow means all primaries are assigned but a replica is not; data is searchable with reduced redundancy. A primary and its replica cannot occupy the same node.
variants.prompt: Disk on the data nodes is nearly full, and replicas stay unassigned. Why?
options: Allocation watermarks prevent placing copies without recovery headroom.
Replicas are optional and never assigned automatically.
optionFeedback: Elasticsearch refuses to allocate shards past its disk watermarks.
Replicas are assigned automatically when a valid node has room.
variants.hint: What does the cluster need in order to restore redundancy?
variants.explanation: Keep disk headroom beyond the arithmetic minimum, or the cluster cannot restore redundancy after a failure.

variants.title: Reindex without mixing contracts
variants.context: Elasticsearch is a derived read model. Reindex into a new generation from a durable change stream, catch up, compare, and move aliases atomically only after explicit release gates pass.
variants.prompt: The products mapping must change. Put the migration in order.

items.text: Create products-v2 with the new mapping, analyzers, and shard plan.
Record a source checkpoint and backfill through the live transformer.
Catch up mutations after the checkpoint and compare counts, samples, relevance, and latency.
Move the read and write aliases atomically after release gates pass.

variants.hint: The alias moves last, and only after the comparison passes.
variants.explanation: Create → backfill → catch up and compare → switch aliases. Keep rollback and snapshots until the old generation’s retention expires.

variants.title: Reindex without mixing contracts
variants.context: Elasticsearch is a derived read model. Reindex into a new generation from a durable change stream, catch up, compare, and move aliases atomically only after explicit release gates pass.
variants.prompt: An analyzer change needs a new generation. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Create the new index with the new analyzer.
Backfill every document from the replayable source from a checkpoint.
Replay mutations since the checkpoint and validate against explicit gates.
Cut traffic over by moving aliases in one atomic step.

variants.hint: Backfill and catch-up both come before any traffic moves.
variants.explanation: Existing segments keep old terms, so a new generation is built from the source of truth and switched atomically.

variants.title: Reindex without mixing contracts
variants.context: Elasticsearch is a derived read model. Reindex into a new generation from a durable change stream, catch up, compare, and move aliases atomically only after explicit release gates pass.
variants.prompt: Search needs rebuilding after a bad transformer bug. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Create a fresh index generation.
Replay the durable change stream from a checkpoint, indexing by stable ID.
Catch up, then compare counts and sampled documents with the old generation.
Switch aliases and keep the old generation for rollback.

variants.hint: A durable outbox lets you rebuild without scraping the live database.
variants.explanation: Replayable events with stable IDs and versions mean a rebuild replaces the same logical documents deterministically.
